title: Leave Brutalism Alone!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore brutalist architecture: its origins in the term beton brut (raw concrete) and the post-WWII rebuilding, the Smithsons and early use of the term by Hans Asplund (Villa Göth, 1949), Reyner Banham's popularization, its spread across Europe, the Eastern Bloc, Japan, Latin America and Africa, and its cheap, repetitive modular design. They discuss why it is widely disliked (dystopian film associations, welfare-state politics, decay and leaks), examples such as Paul Rudolph's Orange County Government Center (torn down), Prentice Women's Hospital, Robin Hood Gardens, the Royal National Theatre, Habitat 67, Hiroshima Peace Center, Hotel Duhau-style Tunisian Hotel Sidi Driss, Geisel Library, and Atlanta's Central Library by Marcel Breuer. A listener mail correction covers military discharge types.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to brutalism
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck welcome listeners, and Josh introduces brutalism as a reviled but misunderstood architecture that is now being reappraised and threatened with demolition.

segments.title: Mexico City temples and brutalism as stripped ornamentation
segments.summary: Chuck describes noticing pyramid-like brutalist buildings in Mexico City that echo Mayan temples, which were originally ornate. Josh explains brutalism is designed without ornamentation.

segments.title: Origin of the term: beton brut and common misconceptions
segments.summary: Josh explains the term does not describe how buildings feel but comes from Le Corbusier's beton brut, meaning raw concrete. They discuss the distinction between modernism and brutalism and whether there are clear principles.

segments.title: Post-war origins with the Smithsons and early use of the term
segments.summary: Chuck credits Peter and Alison Smithson with using bombed-out London rubble as inspiration. Josh notes the Smithsons are credited with establishing the movement, Reyner Banham popularized the term in a review, and Hans Asplund used it in 1949 for Villa Göth in Uppsala.

segments.title: Global spread after World War II and decolonization
segments.summary: Brutalism spread across Europe, the Eastern Bloc, and Japan, including Okinawa, during rebuilding. Chuck links it to decolonization in Latin America and Africa. Josh explains it was cheap and built from repeated standardized units.

segments.title: Repetition, urban housing, and government buildings
segments.summary: The hosts discuss repetitive modular design such as Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation, the move to cities, and why US federal government buildings adopted brutalism, including a note about DC.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before returning to the discussion of Washington, DC.

segments.title: Washington DC, skyscrapers, and materials
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck discuss DC's low skyline and why brutalism suits it, that brutalist towers are rare, and that brutalism can include brick, steel, glass, and wood, such as organic brutalism.

segments.title: Concrete texture and brutally honest design
segments.summary: Josh describes how architects varied the surface of raw concrete with ripples and aggregate, and the idea that brutalism is brutally honest. Chuck connects permanence to government buildings.

segments.title: Defining features and the early hatred of brutalism
segments.summary: Josh lists features: angular, blocky, deep-set fortress-like windows, and self-repeating modules sometimes called fractal. Chuck notes that the Unité d'Habitation was disliked by residents, although the intelligentsia appreciated it.

segments.title: Why brutalism is associated with villains and dystopia
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how brutalist buildings appear in films as villain lairs and dystopian settings, and the irony that these public buildings were meant to be humanizing.

segments.title: Karate Kid Part III, Ennis House, and Frank Lloyd Wright
segments.summary: Chuck recalls Terry Silver's lair in Karate Kid III, which is the Ennis House designed by Frank Lloyd Wright in Los Angeles. They discuss other Wright buildings like the Guggenheim as partially brutalist. Josh notes the house used in the film was Ennis House, not the Haunted Hill house.

segments.title: Political associations and decline with welfare state
segments.summary: Josh says brutalism is associated with public housing and the welfare state, and that the era ended around 1980 with Reagan and Thatcher. Chuck notes the buildings show their age through water damage and staining.

segments.title: Paul Rudolph's Orange County Government Center and other demolitions
segments.summary: Chuck describes the Orange County Government Center in Goshen, New York, by Paul Rudolph, which leaked and was torn down after a cost study. Josh notes a retrofit that disfigured it, and Architectural Record called Rudolph the unluckiest architect. They also mention Bertrand Goldberg's Prentice Women's Hospital in Chicago, which was torn down.

segments.title: Brutalism as symbol of decay and abandonment
segments.summary: Chuck cites writers who describe brutalist buildings as symbols of human abandonment and urban decay, and Josh adds that they show neglect and became symbols of failed welfare. They also discuss the pronunciation of the magazine name.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break to correct magazine names.

segments.title: Paul Rudolph's Goshen building and famous architects' leaks
segments.summary: Josh recalls the Orange County building had eighty-seven roofs and was made of three buildings. They discuss Frank Lloyd Wright's leaking roofs and the tendency to give famous architects too much leeway.

segments.title: Brutalist interior design trends
segments.summary: Chuck suggests that brutalist touches can be used in interior decorating, and Josh says he is not a fan of the trend. Chuck notes exposed concrete, air ducts, and Edison bulbs in modern offices.

segments.title: Brutalism revival and Atlanta Central Library
segments.summary: Chuck says brutalism is making a comeback in the 2020s with some true brutalist houses in Atlanta. Josh describes the 2018 refurbishment of the Central Atlanta Library by Marcel Breuer, which made it closer to his original intentions, and contrasts that with buildings torn down after being voted ugly.

segments.title: Notable brutalist architects
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh name prominent brutalist architects, including Louis Kahn, Paul Rudolph, Marcel Breuer, Ernő Goldfinger and Bertrand Goldberg. They note that Moshe Safdie's Kips Bay Plaza in New York is brutalist, though he is known for other work.

segments.title: Robin Hood Gardens and the Royal National Theatre
segments.summary: Josh describes Robin Hood Gardens by the Smithsons, part of which was demolished while three stories were acquired by the V&A. They discuss Prince Charles's criticism of the Royal National Theatre and Josh's defense of its harmonious lines and site fit.

segments.title: Habitat 67 and the Hiroshima Peace Center
segments.summary: Chuck praises Moshe Safdie's Habitat 67 from Montreal's 1967 World's Fair. Josh recommends the Hiroshima Peace Center by Kenzo Tange, built to preserve memory of the bombing and promote peace.

segments.title: Hiroshima details and Hotel Sidi Driss in Tunisia
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss Hiroshima's preserved bank frame and outdoor museum. Chuck describes the Hotel Sidi Driss in Tunisia, which resembles the sandcrawler from Star Wars, and suggests it may have inspired George Lucas.

segments.title: Geisel Library in San Diego
segments.summary: Josh describes the Geisel Library in San Diego, originally the Central Library, renamed after Audrey Geisel's donation. Chuck notes the building's use of glass, which is unusual for brutalism.

segments.title: Drinking game joke and dystopian brutalist videos
segments.summary: Hosts joke about how often they said brutalist in the episode. Josh recommends Eternal Dystopia's YouTube drone videos featuring dystopian brutalist architecture.

segments.title: Listener mail: military discharge correction
segments.summary: Chuck corrects an earlier mistake from the Nuclear Boy Scout episode that the USS Enterprise was a nuclear submarine, and he apologizes for a wrong claim about military discharge. Listener Scott Oliver explains honorable, general, other than honorable, bad conduct, and dishonorable discharges.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Josh invites listeners to send feedback to the show's email address, and Chuck gives the closing credits.
